title: 2D collisions & restitution
examples: How do I find the final velocities after a collision at an angle?
What does the coefficient of restitution tell us about the collision?
Is momentum always conserved in a 2D collision?

explain.say: Today we look at collisions happening in two dimensions.
We break all velocities into horizontal and vertical parts.
Momentum is conserved separately for both the x and y directions.
The coefficient of restitution, e, relates the relative velocities.
For a perfectly elastic collision, the coefficient e equals one.
In a real-life example, two billiard balls collide on a table.

faq.q: Do I always need to use the coefficient of restitution?
faq.a: You only need it if the collision is not perfectly elastic. If the objects stick together, e is zero.
asks: When is e not equal to one?
What if the energy is lost?

faq.q: Do I calculate the components first or use the coefficient?
faq.a: You must calculate the components first. Then you use the conservation laws for each component.
asks: Do I solve for x and y separately?

faq.q: Does momentum conservation only apply to the horizontal direction?
faq.a: No, momentum is conserved independently in both the horizontal and vertical directions.
asks: Must I treat x and y separately?

faq.q: What is the difference between conservation of momentum and energy?
faq.a: Momentum conservation applies even if energy is lost. Energy conservation requires the collision to be perfectly elastic.

faq.q: If the collision is perfectly inelastic, what is e?
faq.a: If the objects stick together, they move with the same final velocity. In this case, the coefficient e is zero.

facts: In 2D, momentum must be conserved for the x-component and the y-component.
The coefficient of restitution, e, is defined using relative velocities.
For a perfectly elastic collision, e equals one.

quiz.say: Two masses collide at an angle. Which physical law must be used for the horizontal velocities?

options.show: The total momentum in the x-direction must be conserved.
options.say: The total momentum in the x-direction must be conserved.

options.show: The kinetic energy must be conserved.
options.say: The kinetic energy must be conserved.

options.show: The coefficient e must be used.
options.say: The coefficient e must be used.

options.show: The vertical momentum must be zero.
options.say: The vertical momentum must be zero.

quiz.why: Momentum is always conserved in the x-direction unless an external force acts horizontally.

wrong.1: Energy conservation only applies if the collision is perfectly elastic.
wrong.2: The coefficient e relates the relative separation, not just the x-momentum.
wrong.3: The vertical momentum is conserved separately, it is not necessarily zero.

quiz.say: A collision is perfectly inelastic. What is the value of the coefficient of restitution, e?
quiz.why: When objects stick together, their relative separation velocity is zero, making e zero.

wrong.0: The coefficient e must be a positive value between zero and one.
wrong.2: One indicates a perfectly elastic collision where energy is conserved.
wrong.3: The coefficient e cannot be greater than one for physical collisions.

quiz.say: If the relative velocity after collision is less than the relative velocity before collision, what is the value of e?

options.show: e is between zero and one
options.say: e is between zero and one

quiz.why: If energy is lost, the objects do not rebound as strongly, so e is less than one.

wrong.0: A value greater than one suggests energy was gained, which is impossible.
wrong.2: This implies no energy was lost during the collision.
wrong.3: This only happens if the objects stick together completely.
